study: Morck, Stangeland & Yeung, 'Inherited Wealth, Corporate Control, and Economic Growth: The Canadian Disease?'
venue: NBER volume Concentrated Corporate Ownership (ed. Morck), ch. 11, pp. 319-372 (WP 6814, Nov 1998)
country_sample: 41 countries (1993 Forbes billionaires); 246 public firms among Financial Post 500 (1988), Canada
design: cross-country growth regressions; firm-level comparisons vs US industry and matched US firms, 1984-89; event study of 1988 FTA election
headline_finding: Heir wealth/GDP associated with slower growth (75th pct heir wealth = -0.96 pp/yr growth; 90th pct = -1.95 pp/yr); heir-controlled Canadian firms have lower returns on assets/sales, lower labour intensity (more capital-intensive), less R&D; heir firms' shares underperformed on FTA ratification news

study: Morck, Wolfenzon & Yeung, 'Corporate Governance, Economic Entrenchment, and Growth'
headline_finding: pyramids/dual class let families control without commensurate capital; 'economic entrenchment' - controlling families' political influence scales with assets controlled, not owned

study: Smith & Amoako-Adu, 'Management succession and financial performance of family controlled firms'
headline_finding: share prices drop when heirs take charge, especially young heirs (as summarized by MWY 2005; abstract not retrieved)
firms promoting a family CEO underperform on operating profitability and market-to-book; gap largest when family CEO did not attend a selective college

study: Bennedsen, Nielsen, Pérez-González & Wolfenzon, 'Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance'
design: IV: gender of departing CEO's first-born child
headline_finding: family successions cause operating ROA to fall by at least 4 percentage points around CEO transitions; larger in fast-growing, skill-intensive industries

study: Villalonga & Amit, 'How do family ownership, control and management affect firm value?'
headline_finding: family ownership creates value only when founder is CEO or chairman with hired CEO; 'When descendants serve as CEOs, firm value is destroyed'; dual class/pyramids/voting agreements reduce founder premium; 56% of 2nd+ generation firms use control-enhancing mechanisms vs 37% of first-generation
direction_for_heirs: positive for founders / negative for heirs

study: Anderson & Reeb, 'Founding-Family Ownership and Firm Performance: Evidence from the S&P 500'
headline_finding: 'Contrary to our conjecture, we find family firms perform better than nonfamily firms'; family CEO better than outside CEO; nonlinear
direction_for_heirs: positive (counter-evidence; largely founder effect per V&A)

study: Jog, Zhu & Dutta, 'Impact of Restricted Voting Share Structure on Firm Value and Performance'
headline_finding: no evidence that restricted-voting (dual-class) firms have lower value, operating or stock performance, nor expropriation via M&A/dividends

study: Gompers, Ishii & Metrick, 'Extreme Governance: An Analysis of Dual-Class Firms in the United States'
design: OLS and IV (exogenous predictors of dual class)
headline_finding: firm value rises with insiders' cash-flow rights and falls with their voting rights

study: Smart, Thirumalai & Zutter, 'What's in a vote?'
headline_finding: dual-class firms trade at lower prices than single-class at IPO and for 5+ years, without lower subsequent returns; CEO turnover insensitive to performance in duals; unifications create value

study: Cremers, Lauterbach & Pajuste, 'The Life-Cycle of Dual Class Firm Valuations'
headline_finding: dual-class firms have higher valuations around IPO; premium dissipates over time while the voting-equity wedge grows; mild support for age-based sunsets
